newsitem.title: CANADA: Hibernia terminal envisioned as regional utility.
newsitem.headline: Hibernia terminal envisioned as regional utility.

text.p: A transshipment terminal to be built to take in crude oil produced from the massive Hibernia oil project would likely be expanded to handle output from several other future offshore projects, partners in the project said on Thursday.

"We are, as owners, looking at this more along the lines of a utility that is looking at a rate of return that is commensurate with the risk that is associated with the kind of facility that we're putting in place," Norm McIntyre, executive vice president of partner Petro-Canada told reporters.
McIntyre said the return was expected to be 12 to 15 percent.

Three Hibernia partners, whose offshore project is expected to start pumping out 135,000 barrels of oil per day in 1997, said on Thursday they agreed to build the C$100-million terminal near Come By Chance in Newfoundland.
Transshipment is a two-stage transport process for moving oil to market. Oil from offshore production facilities is tranferred to shuttle tankers which carry it to the terminal.
The crude is stored at the transshipment facility until it is tranferred to a conventional tanker and shipped to markets.

Partners in the terminal, which also include Mobil Corp unit Mobil Oil Canada and Chevron Corp unit Chevron Canada Resources, said the 1.5 million barrel facility would initially include one berth to accommodate tankers up to 155,000 dead weight tons.
However, two or more berths could be added in the future.
The parters said the terminal's eventual expansion would be a welcome addition for future oil projects planned for the Grand Banks off the east coast of Canada.
Beyond Hibernia, the region's first project, plans include development of Terra Nova, White Rose and others in the Jean d'Arc Basin.

"Three of the (Hibernia) partners, Mobil, Chevron and Petro-Canada, have mutliple interests on the Grand Banks and our evaluation showed that a transshipment facility closest to the point of production made the most sense for us from an economic standpoint," said Mobil Oil Canada president Jerry Anderson.
McIntyre said Petro-Canada had decided only a few weeks ago to become a transshipment partner.

He said Hibernia's imminent production, the approaching commitment to proceed with Terra Nova, a new generic royalty regime in Newfoundland and Petro-Canada's dominant reserve position in the region combined to lead the company to its decision to climb aboard.
"It gives us the marketing flexibility, not only with our refinery operations in Canada, but other potential points of disposition of our product as we go forward," he said.
Anderson said that with the terminal's close proximity to Vitol 's North Atlantic Refining Ltd refinery at Come By Chance, the plant could take in crude from the new facility.
A deal to link the operations by pipeline had not been worked out, he said.

Newfoundland Premier Brian Tobin, whose province's economy was devastated by the 1992 collapse of its fishing industry, said renewed oil activity in the region was aiding a recovery. The oil development plans are not dependent on government subsidies, as in Newfoundland's exploration boom in the 1970s.

Partners in Hibernia are Petro-Canada with 25 percent, Mobil with 33.125 percent, Chevron with 26.875 percent, Murphy Oil Corp with 6.5 percent and the government of Canada with 8.5 percent. -- Reuters Calgary Bureau 403 531-1624
